ai-1/1.title: Find the decision maker
ai-1/1.teach: Ask what evidence would reveal how the smart speaker decides.
ai-1/1.misconception: A robot body proves the device learns.
ai-1/1.scenario: Six devices are a motion-triggered lamp, a trained photo sorter, a remote-controlled car, a calculator, an unspecified smart speaker and an unspecified robot vacuum.
ai-1/1.question: Classify all six using mechanism evidence. Which two need more information?
ai-1/1.explanation: The lamp uses a fixed rule; the photo sorter uses a learned model; the car follows human commands; the calculator performs arithmetic. The speaker and vacuum need mechanism details. Products can combine mechanisms. A robot body or smart label proves none of them.

ai-1/2.title: From mood to song titles
ai-1/2.teach: Ask students to point to where information changes.
ai-1/2.misconception: Displaying a title means the song is already playing.
ai-1/2.scenario: A playlist helper receives a mood, matches song tags and displays three titles.
ai-1/2.question: Name input, process and output. Is displaying titles the same as playing audio?
ai-1/2.explanation: Input is mood; process is tag matching; output is titles. Audio playback is another step. Matching can use fixed rules; the description alone does not establish machine learning.

ai-1/3.title: Two light readings, one sensor
ai-1/3.teach: Cover the location labels and ask which reading suggests more light under the same settings.
ai-1/3.misconception: A light or sound sensor directly measures happiness.
ai-1/3.scenario: A light sensor reads 15 in a cupboard and 90 near a window. A microphone records a clap.
ai-1/3.question: Which measures a light-related signal? Can either directly measure happiness?
ai-1/3.explanation: The light sensor measures light; the microphone measures sound. Neither directly measures feelings. Units and calibration matter when comparing devices.

ai-1/4.title: Where did the decision come from?
ai-1/4.teach: Give a blue card to the rule follower and ask what instruction is missing.
ai-1/4.misconception: Every possible input has an action even when no rule states one.
ai-1/4.scenario: Sorter A follows a written red-card-left rule. Sorter B is fitted using labelled leaves.
ai-1/4.question: How were their decision processes obtained? Where should A send blue cards?
ai-1/4.explanation: A was explicitly programmed; B learned parameters from examples. Blue-card handling is unspecified, so request a rule. Both systems can fail.

ai-1/5.title: A picture represented by four numbers
ai-1/5.teach: Change the top-left value to 1. Ask what changes in the image and what stays the same.
ai-1/5.misconception: Storing pixel values is the same as recognising an object.
ai-1/5.scenario: A 2 by 2 image has rows [0,1] and [1,0]. Zero means white and one means black.
ai-1/5.question: Draw it, then change the top-left value to 1.
ai-1/5.explanation: Initially top-right and bottom-left are black. The change produces three black squares. Pixel values encode an image; object recognition is a separate interpretation.

ai-1/6.title: Sound samples show changes in amplitude
ai-1/6.teach: Keep microphone distance and settings the same. Ask what larger amplitude tells us, and what it cannot tell us.
ai-1/6.misconception: Larger amplitude identifies the spoken word.
ai-1/6.scenario: A microphone records quiet and loud claps at the same distance and settings.
ai-1/6.question: What waveform difference is expected? Does it reveal a spoken word?
ai-1/6.explanation: The louder clap generally produces larger amplitude. Amplitude is not word meaning. Distance, gain and noise must be controlled.

ai-1/7.title: Use the same label rule for every card
ai-1/7.teach: Mix colours within each shape group and ask whether the shape label changes.
ai-1/7.misconception: Different colours require different shape labels.
ai-1/7.scenario: Six cards show two circles, two triangles and two squares. Sort by shape.
ai-1/7.question: Why can red and blue circles share a label?
ai-1/7.explanation: Both meet the circle definition. Colour does not change the agreed shape label. Apply one definition consistently.

ai-1/8.title: Choose a clue that answers this task
ai-1/8.teach: Show two equally sized leaves with different edges and ask which clue separates them.
ai-1/8.misconception: The biggest visible difference is always the useful feature.
ai-1/8.scenario: Two green leaves have smooth and toothed edges. The task is to distinguish edge types.
ai-1/8.question: Choose the relevant feature and explain why size is insufficient.
ai-1/8.explanation: Edge shape directly addresses the target. Size can vary within both categories. Feature usefulness depends on the task.

ai-1/9.title: Trace a robot's position
ai-1/9.teach: Ask students to predict each position before advancing the trace.
ai-1/9.misconception: Commands work without a starting position or direction.
ai-1/9.scenario: A robot starts on the left of three squares, facing right. It executes MOVE, MOVE, STOP, each MOVE being one square.
ai-1/9.question: Trace the position after each command.
ai-1/9.explanation: Middle, rightmost, unchanged. Direction, distance and starting conditions must be specified.

ai-1/10.title: Does this card have a star?
ai-1/10.teach: Emphasise has a star, then test a card containing both shapes.
ai-1/10.misconception: Has a star means has only a star.
ai-1/10.scenario: If a card has a star, send it to A; otherwise send it to B.
ai-1/10.question: Sort a star, a circle, and a card with both shapes.
ai-1/10.explanation: Star and mixed cards go to A because both have a star. The circle goes to B. The test is has a star, not has only a star.

ai-1/11.title: Repeat with a clear stopping point
ai-1/11.teach: Ask what happens if only three unstamped cards are available.
ai-1/11.misconception: A repeat command can continue without enough input or a stopping rule.
ai-1/11.scenario: Repeat take the next unstamped card and stamp it four times.
ai-1/11.question: How many cards are stamped? What assumption matters?
ai-1/11.explanation: Four, provided four unstamped cards exist and each repeat takes the next one. A limit or end-of-stack check prevents continuing indefinitely.

ai-1/12.title: Repair the earliest missing action
ai-1/12.teach: Run both programs from the same starting square and compare the trace.
ai-1/12.misconception: Changing the destination repairs the program.
ai-1/12.scenario: A robot should go from square one to square three. Its program is MOVE ONE, STOP.
ai-1/12.question: Find the cause and repair one thing.
ai-1/12.explanation: It stops at square two because one move is missing. Add MOVE ONE before STOP and retest from the same start.

ai-1/13.title: Examples suggest a pattern to test
ai-1/13.teach: Ask why one correct new leaf does not prove every future prediction.
ai-1/13.misconception: One successful prediction proves the classifier always works.
ai-1/13.scenario: Training examples label smooth leaves S and toothed leaves T. A new leaf is toothed.
ai-1/13.question: Predict and state the evidence limit.
ai-1/13.explanation: Predict T from the demonstrated edge pattern. One success does not establish broad reliability; use fresh labelled tests including ambiguous cases.

ai-1/14.title: Does the object have wheels?
ai-1/14.teach: Ask whether the intended vehicle category includes boats, independently of the rule.
ai-1/14.misconception: The rule's output defines the true category automatically.
ai-1/14.scenario: A human classifier uses has wheels means vehicle on a bicycle, wheelchair, toy car and boat.
ai-1/14.question: Apply the rule and identify a limitation.
ai-1/14.explanation: The first three receive vehicle; the boat does not. If the intended category includes boats, the rule misses them. Define the category independently of the prediction rule.

ai-1/15.title: Keep the final cards unseen
ai-1/15.teach: Ask when opening the sealed cards would make them part of practice.
ai-1/15.misconception: A familiar practice card is a fresh test.
ai-1/15.lesson: Week 15: Save New Examples for Testing
ai-1/15.scenario: Cards A–F are used for practice. G and H remain sealed.
ai-1/15.question: Which can provide a fresh test, and under what condition?
ai-1/15.explanation: G and H, only if neither influenced teaching or revision. Familiar cases do not establish unseen performance. Keep final test answers separate.

ai-1/16.title: Two different reasons to ask for help
ai-1/16.teach: Ask students to explain each uncertainty cause instead of only saying wrong.
ai-1/16.misconception: Every uncertain case has the same cause.
ai-1/16.scenario: A sorter handles clearly red and clearly blue cards. Purple and very dark cards arrive.
ai-1/16.question: How should it handle each uncertain case?
ai-1/16.explanation: Use a review tray. Purple is outside the clear categories; darkness prevents observation. These are different uncertainty causes.

ai-1/17.title: A prediction becomes checkable evidence

items.label: Tomorrow
items.value: Observe using an agreed rain rule

ai-1/17.teach: Ask when the class can know whether the prediction matched the observation.
ai-1/17.misconception: A prediction is already a fact about tomorrow.
ai-1/17.scenario: A weather helper predicts tomorrow's rain.
ai-1/17.question: Is this a fact about tomorrow? How can it be checked?
ai-1/17.explanation: It is a prediction. Record it now and compare with a predefined rain observation tomorrow. Useful predictions are not guarantees.

ai-1/18.title: Confidence cannot replace evidence
ai-1/18.teach: Ask which evidence establishes correctness and which only describes certainty.
ai-1/18.misconception: A confident answer must be correct.
ai-1/18.scenario: A helper confidently labels a blurred dog photo as cat; the clear original shows a dog.
ai-1/18.question: What does this show?
ai-1/18.explanation: Confidence and correctness differ. A confident error remains wrong. Check evidence, particularly unfamiliar or low-quality inputs.

ai-1/19.title: Count matching book traits
ai-1/19.teach: Ask how the ranking changes if the reader no longer wants adventure.
ai-1/19.misconception: Similarity is a universal measure of book quality.
ai-1/19.scenario: Book A has animals and adventure; B has animals only; C has neither. A reader wants both traits.
ai-1/19.question: Rank by number of matching traits.
ai-1/19.explanation: A scores 2, B 1, C 0. Ranking depends on the chosen traits; it is not a universal measure of book quality.

ai-1/20.title: Recommendations shape future evidence
ai-1/20.teach: Ask what one choice fails to tell us about the reader.
ai-1/20.misconception: One chosen book reveals every interest.
ai-1/20.scenario: A recommender suggests adventure books after one adventure-book choice.
ai-1/20.question: Explain its evidence and limitation.
ai-1/20.explanation: The past choice supports considering adventure, but does not capture every interest. Ask for feedback and offer variety.

ai-1/21.title: Check suspicious data before changing it
ai-1/21.teach: Ask why crossing out a zero without checking the source invents data.
ai-1/21.misconception: An unusual value should silently become the number we expect.
ai-1/21.scenario: Ordinary pencil lengths are recorded as 12 cm, 14 cm, blank and 130 cm.
ai-1/21.question: What needs checking? May 130 silently become 13?
ai-1/21.explanation: Investigate missing and unusually large values using the source and units. Do not invent a repair. Document verified corrections.

ai-1/22.title: Training examples can leave gaps
ai-1/22.teach: Ask whether copying the one dark photo nine times adds nine new situations.
ai-1/22.misconception: Repeated copies provide the same variety as fresh examples.
ai-1/22.scenario: Training includes nine daylight leaf photos and one low-light photo.
ai-1/22.question: What intended-use gap is present?
ai-1/22.explanation: Low light is poorly represented. Add varied, correctly labelled low-light examples if that use is intended. Copies of one photo do not add equivalent variety.

ai-1/23.title: Compare success under two conditions
ai-1/23.teach: Ask students to shade the successful cases, then name a controlled follow-up test.
ai-1/23.misconception: Different rates prove noise is the only cause.
ai-1/23.scenario: A voice system succeeds on 8/10 quiet and 4/10 noisy recordings.
ai-1/23.question: Compare and propose the next investigation.
ai-1/23.explanation: The rates differ. Test more varied recordings under controlled conditions and inspect other factors before claiming a cause.

ai-1/24.title: Collect only what the book task needs
ai-1/24.teach: Ask which decision each proposed field would help make.
ai-1/24.misconception: More personal data always makes the helper better.
ai-1/24.scenario: A genre-based book helper asks for genre, home address and a photograph.
ai-1/24.question: Which fields are necessary?
ai-1/24.explanation: Genre is relevant; address and photo are unnecessary for the stated task. Collecting less reduces exposure.

ai-1/25.title: Choose the operation that fits
ai-1/25.teach: Ask how an invented passage differs from finding the real handbook.
ai-1/25.misconception: A fluent invented passage counts as retrieval.
ai-1/25.scenario: A learner needs a new poem, 18+7, and a passage from the class handbook.
ai-1/25.question: Choose the operation for each.
ai-1/25.explanation: Generate the poem, calculate 25, retrieve the actual passage. Inventing a fluent passage is not retrieval.

ai-1/26.title: Make a poem request checkable
ai-1/26.teach: Ask partners to check each condition separately after writing a poem.
ai-1/26.misconception: Make it good is a complete instruction.
ai-1/26.scenario: The prompt says make it good; the desired output is a four-line rain poem using simple words.
ai-1/26.question: Write a checkable prompt.
ai-1/26.explanation: Ask for exactly four lines about rain in simple vocabulary. Check line count, topic and vocabulary separately.

ai-1/27.title: Six groups of four make twenty-four
ai-1/27.teach: Count four six times, then compare with the claimed answer 28.
ai-1/27.misconception: Confident wording makes incorrect arithmetic correct.
ai-1/27.scenario: An answer says six groups of four make 28.
ai-1/27.question: Verify independently.
ai-1/27.explanation: Six times four is 24. Draw six groups or add four six times. Confident wording does not change arithmetic.

ai-1/28.title: A suggestion must stop at the approval gate
ai-1/28.teach: Ask students to point to the exact step where permission is needed.
ai-1/28.misconception: Permission to suggest also permits action.
ai-1/28.scenario: An assistant may suggest object locations; a teacher must approve moving valuable equipment.
ai-1/28.question: What may happen without approval?
ai-1/28.explanation: It may suggest a location within its role. Moving equipment requires actual teacher approval.

ai-1/29.title: Solve the need before selecting technology
ai-1/29.teach: Ask which observation would justify trying the simpler solution first.
ai-1/29.scenario: Shared markers are often lost because tray labels are unclear.
ai-1/29.question: State the need before selecting AI.
ai-1/29.explanation: Students need to return markers correctly and quickly. Test clearer labels before proposing a model.

ai-1/30.title: Design a sorter with only relevant inputs

items.label: Review
items.value: Ask a person when material is unclear

ai-1/30.teach: Ask why a home address cannot help this material decision.
ai-1/30.misconception: A sorter needs all information about the person holding the object.
ai-1/30.scenario: A sorter suggests paper or plastic trays using material observations.
ai-1/30.question: Name an input, output and unnecessary input.
ai-1/30.explanation: Input: material or a suitable image. Output: tray suggestion. Home address is unnecessary. Uncertain material needs review.

ai-1/31.title: Otherwise includes every remaining case
ai-1/31.teach: Trace glass through the original paper/otherwise rule and locate the wrong turn.
ai-1/31.misconception: Otherwise means only the category I had in mind.
ai-1/31.scenario: A rule sends paper to P and everything else to M. Inputs include paper, metal and glass.
ai-1/31.question: Trace glass and repair the rule.
ai-1/31.explanation: Glass incorrectly goes to M. Add an explicit metal check and a glass or review branch. Otherwise includes all remaining cases.

ai-1/32.title: Act out a paper prototype

items.label: Token
items.value: Place in paper, plastic or review tray

ai-1/32.teach: Ask which person is simulating each part of the system.
ai-1/32.misconception: A paper simulation proves a learned model was trained.
ai-1/32.scenario: A paper prototype has input cards, decision cards and paper, plastic and review trays.
ai-1/32.question: How can a learner simulate it?
ai-1/32.explanation: Read input, follow written decisions and place a token in a tray. Record the trace. Human simulation does not establish model training.

ai-1/33.title: Report the cases actually tested
ai-1/33.teach: Ask students to keep the failed case and trace its cause.
ai-1/33.misconception: Three successes justify a claim about all unfamiliar inputs.
ai-1/33.scenario: Four routine cases are chosen before testing. Three are correct.
ai-1/33.question: What can be reported?
ai-1/33.explanation: 3/4 on those cases. Preserve the failure and trace its cause. This does not guarantee unfamiliar-case performance.

ai-1/34.title: Test conditions that reveal limitations

items.label: Expected action
items.value: Declare tray or review before testing

ai-1/34.teach: Ask how the team would know whether a review result was appropriate.
ai-1/34.misconception: A test counts as passed whenever the team likes the answer afterwards.
ai-1/34.lesson: Week 34: Test Edge Cases and Fairness
ai-1/34.scenario: A sorter handles clean paper but fails on crumpled paper and mixed packaging.
ai-1/34.question: Design revealing tests.
ai-1/34.explanation: Use separately labelled clean, crumpled and mixed cases with expected outputs or review actions declared first. Compare conditions.

ai-1/35.title: A fair comparison changes one cause

items.label: Confounded revision
items.value: Lighting, labels and rules all changed

items.label: Controlled revision
items.value: Change one planned factor and retest

ai-1/35.teach: Ask which changed factor caused the improvement and why the evidence cannot isolate it.
ai-1/35.misconception: Fewer errors identify the cause even when everything changed.
ai-1/35.scenario: The team changes lighting, labels and rules together; errors fall from four to one.
ai-1/35.question: Can it identify the cause of improvement?
ai-1/35.explanation: No. Several factors changed. Compare one planned change at a time with controlled conditions.

ai-1/36.title: Defend a claim with a complete trace

items.label: Output
items.value: Show the tray or review result

items.label: Evidence
items.value: Report six classroom passes and limits

ai-1/36.teach: Ask the presenter to demonstrate an uncertain case as well as a success.
ai-1/36.misconception: Six passes prove the system is always correct.
ai-1/36.scenario: The expo poster says always correct after six classroom passes.
ai-1/36.question: Write a defensible claim.
ai-1/36.explanation: Report six specified passes with conditions and limits. Show an input, decision trace, output and test record, including an uncertain case.

ai-2/1.title: Make hidden instructions explicit
ai-2/1.teach: Act literally and ask which instruction must name its object.
ai-2/1.misconception: Close it is precise even when no object is specified.
ai-2/1.scenario: A sandwich algorithm says add spread, close it, cut it, without stating materials or directions.
ai-2/1.question: Expose assumptions and write a precise paper simulation.
ai-2/1.explanation: Use two paper bread squares, mark a spoon-sized spread area on one, place the second on top and draw a diagonal cut. State materials and order. No real food or sharp tools are needed.

ai-2/2.title: Decompose a recommendation into records
ai-2/2.teach: Ask what inspectable output each step leaves for the next.
ai-2/2.misconception: A large goal can be tested without defining its steps.
ai-2/2.scenario: A class wants to recommend one of five library books.
ai-2/2.question: Decompose the goal into checkable steps.
ai-2/2.explanation: Collect preferences, record book traits, score each with a declared rule, handle ties and explain the suggestion. Each step produces an inspectable record.

ai-2/3.title: Test strict and inclusive page boundaries
ai-2/3.teach: Put 100 and 200 on the boundary and ask which comparison includes each.
ai-2/3.misconception: Less than and less than or equal to mean the same thing.
ai-2/3.scenario: If pages<100 choose Short; otherwise if pages<=200 choose Medium; otherwise Long.
ai-2/3.question: Classify 99,100,200,201 pages.
ai-2/3.explanation: Short, Medium, Medium, Long. Strict and inclusive boundaries and branch order matter.

ai-2/4.title: Keep the state after each instruction
ai-2/4.teach: Ask which value is compared with four before subtraction occurs.
ai-2/4.misconception: The comparison uses the final value rather than the current value.
ai-2/4.scenario: Set score=2; add 3; if score>4 subtract 1; double score.
ai-2/4.question: Trace every value.
ai-2/4.explanation: 2,5,4,8. The comparison is evaluated at 5 before subtraction.

ai-2/5.title: A loop must progress toward stopping
ai-2/5.teach: Remove the update in a paper trace and ask why the loop would not stop.
ai-2/5.misconception: Repeating a check automatically changes the value.
ai-2/5.scenario: Start n=0; while n<3, add 1 and record n.
ai-2/5.question: List records and stopping condition.
ai-2/5.explanation: 1,2,3. The next comparison is false. The update makes progress toward termination.

ai-2/6.title: Put the addition inside the condition
ai-2/6.teach: Test zero, one and two matches, expecting zero, two and four points.
ai-2/6.misconception: Every visited trait should earn points.
ai-2/6.scenario: Award two points per matching trait. A bug awards two for every trait.
ai-2/6.question: Test one match and one nonmatch.
ai-2/6.explanation: Expected 2; buggy result 4. Put the addition inside the match condition. Test zero, one and two matches for 0,2,4.

ai-2/7.title: A field has a meaning and a type
ai-2/7.teach: Ask why a field named Pages is not enough to make ninety numeric data.
ai-2/7.misconception: A column heading guarantees valid values.
ai-2/7.lesson: Week 7: Rows Columns and Data Types
ai-2/7.scenario: Fields are Title, Pages and Borrowed; a row contains River, ninety and yes.
ai-2/7.question: Assign intended types and a repair.
ai-2/7.explanation: Text, numeric and Boolean. Confirm ninety means 90, then convert and record the change; use a consistent Boolean representation.

ai-2/8.title: Define Short before labelling books
ai-2/8.teach: Ask two annotators to apply fewer than 100 independently.
ai-2/8.misconception: A 100-page book is Short under a fewer-than-100 definition.
ai-2/8.scenario: Short means fewer than 100 pages. Two annotators disagree about a 100-page book.
ai-2/8.question: Resolve the label.
ai-2/8.explanation: It is not Short under the stated definition. Agree operational boundaries before labelling.

ai-2/9.title: Useful evidence versus a shortcut
ai-2/9.teach: Move a book to a new shelf and ask whether its animal label should change.
ai-2/9.misconception: A correlation in the classroom collection is a dependable defining feature.
ai-2/9.scenario: Target: includes animal characters. Fields: animal tag, cover colour and shelf number.
ai-2/9.question: Choose useful evidence and possible distractions.
ai-2/9.explanation: An accurate animal tag directly addresses the target. Colour and shelf can produce accidental shortcuts. Test on new books.

ai-2/10.title: Both conditions must pass
ai-2/10.teach: Ask students to mark both Boolean results for each book.
ai-2/10.misconception: Passing either condition is enough for AND.
ai-2/10.scenario: Recommend if adventure AND pages<150; otherwise Other.
ai-2/10.question: Trace A=(adventure,120), B=(adventure,180), C=(science,90).
ai-2/10.explanation: A is Recommend. B fails length; C fails genre. Show both conditions.

ai-2/11.title: Separate development from fresh evaluation
ai-2/11.teach: Ask when a repeatedly inspected test set becomes part of development.
ai-2/11.misconception: A score on development examples measures unseen performance.
ai-2/11.scenario: A rule is developed and evaluated using the same books A–H.
ai-2/11.question: Why does this not establish unseen performance?
ai-2/11.explanation: Those cases influenced the rule. Reserve different labelled books that do not influence construction or revision.

ai-2/12.title: All scored cases belong in the denominator
ai-2/12.teach: Ask students to locate the three errors among the twelve cases.
ai-2/12.misconception: Accuracy divides correct cases by only the successful cases.
ai-2/12.scenario: Nine of twelve held-out classifications are correct.
ai-2/12.question: Compute accuracy and state the denominator.
ai-2/12.explanation: 9/12=3/4=75%. Count all scored cases, including errors.

ai-2/13.title: Name outcomes using actual and predicted labels
ai-2/13.teach: Define positive as should recommend before naming any cell.
ai-2/13.misconception: False positive means a negative prediction.
ai-2/13.scenario: Positive means should recommend. Actual/predicted pairs are yes/yes, no/yes, yes/no, no/no.
ai-2/13.question: Name the four outcomes.
ai-2/13.explanation: True positive, false positive, false negative, true negative. Define positive before naming errors.

ai-2/14.title: A decision tree can stop early
ai-2/14.teach: Trace a 90-page science book and ask whether the second question is needed.
ai-2/14.misconception: Every input visits every question in a tree.
ai-2/14.scenario: First ask animal book? If no, Other. If yes, ask pages<100; yes gives Short Animal, no gives Longer Animal.
ai-2/14.question: Trace 90-page animal and science books.
ai-2/14.explanation: The animal book reaches Short Animal; science reaches Other after the first question.

ai-2/15.title: Choose a question that separates the target
ai-2/15.teach: Ask why a question can be accurate yet uninformative for the target.
ai-2/15.misconception: Any visible feature is equally useful for splitting groups.
ai-2/15.scenario: Eight blue cards contain four circles and four triangles; target is shape.
ai-2/15.question: Which question is more useful: blue or circle?
ai-2/15.explanation: Circle separates target groups. Blue puts every card in one branch. Usefulness depends on the task and examples.

ai-2/16.title: Perfect recall can hide weak transfer
ai-2/16.teach: Ask what evidence is still needed before preferring an untested simpler rule.
ai-2/16.misconception: A simpler rule is automatically better without testing.
ai-2/16.scenario: Rule A memorises six training book names. It scores 6/6 familiar and 2/6 new. Rule B uses relevant traits but is untested.
ai-2/16.question: What does the evidence support?
ai-2/16.explanation: A shows weak transfer. B might generalise better but requires testing; simplicity is not proof.

ai-2/17.title: An outlier needs investigation
ai-2/17.teach: Ask what source check would distinguish a typo from a genuinely long book.
ai-2/17.misconception: Every outlier is erroneous and should be deleted.
ai-2/17.question: Is 900 automatically wrong?
ai-2/17.explanation: No. It is an outlier, but may be a real large book. Check catalogue, units and entry process.

ai-2/18.title: Missing is different from zero

items.label: Partial score
items.value: Use a documented policy with uncertainty

ai-2/18.teach: Ask how a silent zero would affect a short-book score.
ai-2/18.misconception: A missing measurement is a measured zero.
ai-2/18.scenario: Genre is known, but page count is missing and length affects recommendation score.
ai-2/18.question: Choose transparent handling.
ai-2/18.explanation: Retrieve or ask for the count, or use a documented partial-score policy with uncertainty. Do not silently insert zero.

ai-2/19.title: Who was left out of the survey?
ai-2/19.teach: Ask how membership selects for the very preference being measured.
ai-2/19.misconception: A convenient club sample represents every school reader.
ai-2/19.scenario: Only adventure-club members answer a school reading survey.
ai-2/19.question: Explain the sampling problem.
ai-2/19.explanation: Membership selects for a relevant interest. Include relevant grades and interests with appropriate data practices.

ai-2/20.title: Repair coverage with varied examples
ai-2/20.teach: Ask what evaluation evidence should be collected for both interests after repair.
ai-2/20.misconception: More copies of the same poetry example solve representation.
ai-2/20.scenario: Training has eighteen adventure readers and two poetry readers; many intended users prefer poetry.
ai-2/20.question: Propose repair and evaluation.
ai-2/20.explanation: Collect varied relevant poetry examples with consistent labels. Compare both interests on separate evaluation cases before and after repair.

ai-2/21.title: Count differing traits from query [1,0]
ai-2/21.teach: Ask why a smaller distance means greater similarity under this rule.
ai-2/21.misconception: Largest distance identifies the nearest neighbour.
ai-2/21.scenario: Traits are [animals,adventure]. A=[1,1], B=[1,0], C=[0,0]; query=[1,0].
ai-2/21.question: Use number of differing traits as distance.
ai-2/21.explanation: Distances: A=1, B=0, C=1. B is nearest with equal feature weights.

ai-2/22.title: A nearest-neighbour tie needs a policy
ai-2/22.teach: Use query [0,1] and ask why k=1 still needs a tie policy.
ai-2/22.misconception: Nearest-neighbour classification always has one unique nearest example.
ai-2/22.scenario: A=[1,1] liked, B=[1,0] disliked, C=[0,0] disliked; query=[0,1].
ai-2/22.question: Find nearest neighbours using differing-trait distance and k=1.
ai-2/22.explanation: A and C tie at distance one; B is distance two. Conflicting nearest labels require a predefined tie policy or uncertainty.

ai-2/23.title: Weighted preferences determine the score
ai-2/23.teach: Award two for genre and one for length, then ask what a different weight would change.
ai-2/23.misconception: Chosen scoring weights express universal reader preferences.
ai-2/23.scenario: Score=2 times genre match + length match. A matches both, B genre only, C length only.
ai-2/23.question: Score and rank.
ai-2/23.explanation: A=3, B=2, C=1. Weights encode a chosen preference, not universal reader truth.

ai-2/24.title: Exposure affects the feedback you collect
ai-2/24.teach: Ask whether no poetry clicks prove a dislike of unseen poetry books.
ai-2/24.misconception: Clicks reveal preferences independently of what was displayed.
ai-2/24.scenario: A recommender shows only adventure books, uses clicks to learn and then shows more adventure.
ai-2/24.question: Explain the feedback loop.
ai-2/24.explanation: Exposure affects clicks; clicks affect future exposure. Record what was shown and offer controlled variety.

ai-2/25.title: One word can have different token counts
ai-2/25.teach: Count three pieces versus one and label both as toy tokenisers.
ai-2/25.misconception: A word always equals one token in every model.
ai-2/25.scenario: Toy tokenizer A splits rainbows as [rain][bow][s]; B uses [rainbows].
ai-2/25.question: Count tokens and state the limit of the example.
ai-2/25.explanation: Three versus one. Token count depends on tokenizer; tokens need not equal words or letters.

ai-2/26.title: Locate the first error in a voice pipeline

items.label: Rank
items.value: Wrong input can produce a wrong suggestion

ai-2/26.teach: Ask students to inspect the transcript before blaming the ranking rule.
ai-2/26.misconception: A correct ranking step repairs a wrong transcription.
ai-2/26.scenario: A voice book helper transcribes speech, extracts preference, then ranks books.
ai-2/26.question: Where can a wrong suggestion begin?
ai-2/26.explanation: Transcription can mishear poetry and pass the wrong preference downstream. Check intermediate results.

ai-2/27.title: Three operations in one book helper
ai-2/27.teach: Ask what each operation produces and how its output can be checked.
ai-2/27.misconception: All computer outputs are generated text.
ai-2/27.scenario: A labels genre; B writes a new blurb; C computes 24/6.
ai-2/27.question: Distinguish operations.
ai-2/27.explanation: A predicts a category, B generates text, C calculates 4. Products may combine them.

ai-2/28.title: Compare prompts under the same conditions

items.label: Prompt B
items.value: Add under 100 pages and explain the match

ai-2/28.teach: Ask which evidence would show that the added instruction helped.
ai-2/28.misconception: Different catalogues give a fair comparison of the prompt alone.
ai-2/28.scenario: Prompt B adds under 100 pages and explain the match to Prompt A. Both use a catalogue.
ai-2/28.question: Design a fair comparison.
ai-2/28.explanation: Use identical requests, catalogue and scoring criteria. Check constraint compliance and supported explanation; repeat stochastic outputs when relevant.

ai-2/29.title: Check the claim against the exact edition

items.label: Resolution
items.value: Verify edition and cite the correct record

ai-2/29.teach: Ask why the edition identifier matters before correcting the number.
ai-2/29.misconception: Any record for the same title verifies every edition.
ai-2/29.scenario: An answer says 80 pages, but the catalogue for that edition says 120.
ai-2/29.question: What evidence guides correction?
ai-2/29.explanation: Check the exact edition and authoritative catalogue record. Record the supporting source.

ai-2/30.title: Tools operate within granted permissions
ai-2/30.teach: Ask where find a book and tell my class crosses the current permission boundary.
ai-2/30.misconception: Permission to draft includes permission to send.
ai-2/30.scenario: An agent may search an approved catalogue and draft suggestions, but not send messages.
ai-2/30.question: Trace find a short science book and tell my class.
ai-2/30.explanation: Search and draft are permitted; sending needs authorisation or an approved permission change.

ai-2/31.title: Put approval after evidence and before action
ai-2/31.teach: Ask what the teacher needs to see to make a meaningful decision.
ai-2/31.misconception: Silence or a draft is equivalent to posting approval.
ai-2/31.scenario: Posting a recommendation requires teacher review.
ai-2/31.question: Place the approval gate.
ai-2/31.explanation: After draft and evidence are visible, before posting; include content and destination. No approval means no post.

ai-2/32.title: Turn a project goal into acceptance tests

items.label: Catalogue
items.value: Suggestion must be one of ten approved books

ai-2/32.teach: Ask students to define expected behaviour before trying each request.
ai-2/32.misconception: A project is successful whenever it produces a book title.
ai-2/32.lesson: Week 32: Project Problem and Success Test
ai-2/32.scenario: A project recommends from ten approved books using genre and length.
ai-2/32.question: Define acceptance tests.
ai-2/32.explanation: Verify book existence, hard constraints, correct scoring explanations, tie handling and no-match behaviour on predefined requests.

ai-2/33.title: Build and expose the scoring calculation
ai-2/33.teach: Use score equals two times genre match plus length match. Ask what must be displayed to reproduce the winner.
ai-2/33.misconception: A winner is transparent without its flags, formula or scores.
ai-2/33.scenario: A has flags (1,1), B=(1,0), C=(0,1); score=2g+l.
ai-2/33.question: Compute the winner and evidence to display.
ai-2/33.explanation: A wins at 3; B=2; C=1. Show flags, formula, scores and explanation; declare tie policy.

ai-2/34.title: Compare success for different interests
ai-2/34.teach: Ask students to investigate catalogue coverage and scoring before claiming a cause.
ai-2/34.misconception: Twelve tests prove the cause of the group difference.
ai-2/34.scenario: A recommender satisfies 5/6 adventure requests and 3/6 poetry requests.
ai-2/34.question: Compare and investigate.
ai-2/34.explanation: Rates are 5/6 and 3/6. Inspect catalogue coverage, labels and scoring; twelve tests do not establish cause.

ai-2/35.title: Improve with comparable evidence
ai-2/35.teach: Ask why replacing difficult cases with easier cases invalidates the comparison.
ai-2/35.misconception: A higher score proves improvement even when the test changed.
ai-2/35.scenario: A repair raises success from 7/10 to 9/10 on the same validation set.
ai-2/35.question: What belongs in the improvement claim?
ai-2/35.explanation: Confirm fixed criteria, inspect remaining and introduced failures, then test the chosen version on fresh final cases.

ai-2/36.title: Defend a transparent recommender

items.label: Logic
items.value: Show a score and tie decision

items.label: Limits
items.value: Demonstrate a missing or uncertain case

ai-2/36.teach: Ask a reviewer to challenge one weight and trace the effect.
ai-2/36.misconception: A successful demo proves every reader will like the suggestion.
ai-2/36.scenario: An expo claim says the recommender knows everybody's favourite book after twelve tests.
ai-2/36.question: Rewrite the defence.
ai-2/36.explanation: Explain trait-based ranking, report the twelve outcomes and limits, and demonstrate no-match handling. It cannot know unstated preferences.

ai-3/1.title: Three outputs need three different checks
ai-3/1.teach: Ask which operation creates wording and which computes an exact arithmetic result.
ai-3/1.misconception: Every output from an assistant is the same kind of operation.
ai-3/1.scenario: A tool labels a question biology, writes a new question and computes 7 times 8.
ai-3/1.question: Identify each operation.
ai-3/1.explanation: Labelling selects a category; generation creates text; calculation returns 56. Generated questions need factual and instructional checks.

ai-3/2.title: A toy next-token probability distribution
ai-3/2.teach: Use five rain, three sun and two snow slips. Ask why rain is most likely but not certain.
ai-3/2.misconception: A token probability is a truth score for the whole sentence.
ai-3/2.scenario: A toy next-token distribution is rain .5, sun .3, snow .2.
ai-3/2.question: Check total and interpret the largest value.
ai-3/2.explanation: Total is 1. Rain is most likely, not guaranteed under sampling. Token probability is not whole-sentence truth.

ai-3/3.title: Nine requested tokens exceed eight spaces
ai-3/3.teach: Ask which instructions and source evidence must survive when shortening the input.
ai-3/3.misconception: All earlier text always remains available to the model.
ai-3/3.scenario: A toy window holds eight tokens; prompt uses six and quotation uses three.
ai-3/3.question: Does it fit? What should be preserved?
ai-3/3.explanation: Nine exceeds eight. Shorten or select material while preserving essential instructions and evidence. Real systems also have output-budget rules.

ai-3/4.title: Variability and quality are separate
ai-3/4.teach: Ask students to use the same rubric on repeated outputs.
ai-3/4.scenario: One prompt produces three different valid quiz questions.
ai-3/4.question: Does variability mean failure?
ai-3/4.explanation: No. Sampling can vary outputs. Score correctness, relevance and format over repeated trials; consistency differs from quality.

ai-3/5.title: A prompt contract makes checking possible
ai-3/5.teach: Ask students to locate support for every bullet as well as count the bullets.
ai-3/5.scenario: Summarise a supplied passage in exactly three bullets using only passage facts.
ai-3/5.question: Define the contract and acceptance checks.
ai-3/5.explanation: Input: passage. Task: summary. Constraints: three bullets, source-only claims. Check count and every claim's support.

ai-3/6.title: Score criteria separately
ai-3/6.teach: Ask which missing criterion would move the total from two to three points.
ai-3/6.misconception: An understandable answer needs no evidence.
ai-3/6.scenario: A rubric gives one point each for correctness, evidence and clarity. An answer is correct and clear but unsupported.
ai-3/6.question: Score and give feedback.
ai-3/6.explanation: 2/3. Ask for supporting evidence, then verify claim-to-source support.

ai-3/7.title: Revise one cause and retest

items.label: Revise
items.value: Simpler vocabulary and one concrete example

ai-3/7.teach: Ask what needs to stay fixed to assess the revision.
ai-3/7.misconception: Changing the passage and prompt together isolates the prompt's effect.
ai-3/7.scenario: A factually correct explanation is too difficult for a nine-year-old.
ai-3/7.question: Make and test one focused revision.
ai-3/7.explanation: Constrain vocabulary and request a concrete example. Compare readability and factual preservation on the same passages.

ai-3/8.title: Type correctness is not factual correctness
ai-3/8.teach: Ask why removing quotation marks fixes the type but does not verify the book.
ai-3/8.scenario: Schema requires title text and pages number. Output is {"title":"River","pages":"80"}.
ai-3/8.question: Diagnose the shape error.
ai-3/8.explanation: Pages is a string, not a number. Use numeric 80. Structure validation does not verify the real page count.

ai-3/9.title: Evaluate prompts on the same questions
ai-3/9.teach: Ask why attractive formatting should be scored separately from passing the task.
ai-3/9.misconception: The more attractive answer is necessarily the more correct one.
ai-3/9.scenario: On five fixed questions, A passes four and B passes three; B looks more attractive.
ai-3/9.question: What conclusion is supported?
ai-3/9.explanation: A has 4/5 versus B's 3/5 on this set. Appearance is separate. Broaden cases and repeat stochastic trials before generalising.

ai-3/10.title: A generated image does not document an event
ai-3/10.teach: Ask what a realistic generated scene can establish about a real event.
ai-3/10.scenario: A generator creates a realistic fictional bicycle beside a tree.
ai-3/10.question: How does this differ from event photography?
ai-3/10.explanation: It synthesises an image from learned patterns and instructions; it does not document that event. Many systems denoise iteratively, but architectures vary.

ai-3/11.title: Map the brief to regions
ai-3/11.teach: Ask students to check subjects, relative sizes and positions separately.
ai-3/11.misconception: Including both objects is enough to satisfy their placement instructions.
ai-3/11.scenario: Brief: large tree left, small bicycle right, open sky above. Output puts bicycle left.
ai-3/11.question: Create a visual checklist.
ai-3/11.explanation: Check subjects, relative size, positions and sky separately. The position violates composition even if subjects exist.

ai-3/12.title: Trace a speech error through the system
ai-3/12.teach: Ask which intermediate representation needs confirmation.
ai-3/12.misconception: Correct arithmetic can recover a misheard input automatically.
ai-3/12.scenario: A speech tool hears fifteen as fifty, then calculates correctly using fifty.
ai-3/12.question: Where did the error enter?
ai-3/12.explanation: Transcription supplied the wrong number. Confirm the transcript or ask for clarification. Correct arithmetic cannot repair wrong input.

ai-3/13.title: Separate visible and off-frame claims

items.label: Evidence limit
items.value: Image cannot settle the off-frame claim

ai-3/13.teach: Cover the caption and ask what the picture alone establishes.
ai-3/13.misconception: An unseen claim becomes verified when placed beside a picture.
ai-3/13.scenario: An image shows three plants; caption claims a fourth outside the frame.
ai-3/13.question: What can the image establish?
ai-3/13.explanation: Three visible plants. It cannot settle an off-frame claim. Attribute claims and preserve missing evidence.

ai-3/14.title: Different failures require different checks
ai-3/14.teach: Ask which check catches a real citation attached to an invented quote.
ai-3/14.misconception: One working source link verifies the whole response.
ai-3/14.scenario: An answer invents a quotation, cites a source lacking it and supplies an impossible date.
ai-3/14.question: Separate the failures and checks.
ai-3/14.explanation: Check exact quote text, claim-to-source support and calendar consistency independently. Each failure needs its own correction.

ai-3/15.title: Follow a summary back to its evidence
ai-3/15.teach: Ask why an original source still needs critical evaluation.
ai-3/15.misconception: An original report is automatically infallible.
ai-3/15.scenario: An original experiment report and an anonymous unlinked summary describe a method.
ai-3/15.question: Where should verification begin?
ai-3/15.explanation: Read the original method, scope and limitations. Original does not mean infallible; summaries may omit conditions.

ai-3/16.title: Verify a percentage independently
ai-3/16.teach: Shade fifteen of twenty boxes, then separately verify the impossible date February 30.
ai-3/16.misconception: Fluent writing means the numbers and dates were checked.
ai-3/16.scenario: An answer says 15/20=80% and sets a deadline of February 30.
ai-3/16.question: Verify both.
ai-3/16.explanation: 15/20=75%. February 30 is invalid in the Gregorian calendar. Check the intended deadline from its authority rather than guessing.

ai-3/17.title: Retrieval creates an inspectable evidence trail

items.label: Verification
items.value: Check the paragraph supports the answer

ai-3/17.teach: Ask what can be inspected in one workflow that is absent from the other.
ai-3/17.misconception: Retrieval guarantees the evidence is used correctly.
ai-3/17.scenario: One assistant answers without search; another retrieves a handbook paragraph.
ai-3/17.question: Compare evidence trails.
ai-3/17.explanation: The first uses learned patterns without an inspected source. The second supplies a passage that can be checked. Retrieval still does not guarantee correct use.

ai-3/18.title: Use the passage that answers the question
ai-3/18.teach: Ask why note B about the returns box does not support the opening time.
ai-3/18.misconception: Any retrieved library note supports every library claim.
ai-3/18.scenario: Note A says library opens at 9. Note B says returns go in the blue box.
ai-3/18.question: Answer opening time with evidence.
ai-3/18.explanation: Answer 9 with note A. Retrieval supplies evidence and generation phrases it. B does not support opening time.

ai-3/19.title: Choose a narrow, testable contribution
ai-3/19.teach: Ask when a simple index already solves the user need.
ai-3/19.misconception: A product must answer everything to be useful.
ai-3/19.lesson: Week 19: User Need and AI Contribution
ai-3/19.scenario: Learners struggle to locate definitions in an approved chapter; a proposed chatbot answers everything.
ai-3/19.question: Narrow the need and AI contribution.
ai-3/19.explanation: Help locate and explain chapter definitions with references and unsupported-question handling. Compare a simple index or search first.

ai-3/20.title: Update only the state the user changed
ai-3/20.teach: Ask which field changes and which should remain.
ai-3/20.misconception: A style change automatically changes the topic.
ai-3/20.scenario: State stores topic=plants and reading_level=beginner. User requests advanced explanation.
ai-3/20.question: What changes?
ai-3/20.explanation: Update reading level, retain topic unless changed. Keep only necessary state with correction/reset. Context does not guarantee permanent memory.

ai-3/21.title: Choose a tool for each subtask
ai-3/21.teach: Ask what evidence accompanies the retrieved definition.
ai-3/21.misconception: A tool result can be used without checking its inputs or relevance.
ai-3/21.scenario: An assistant has calculator and source-search tools. Request: 12 times 9 and habitat definition from a class pack.
ai-3/21.question: Choose and verify tools.
ai-3/21.explanation: Calculator returns 108; search retrieves the definition. Verify inputs, outputs and supporting passage before answering.

ai-3/22.title: Validate the API response before using it
ai-3/22.teach: Ask which check rejects valid JSON for book B8.
ai-3/22.misconception: A parseable response must belong to the requested item.
ai-3/22.scenario: Request is for B7; response is {"id":"B7","pages":120}. Another response has malformed JSON.
ai-3/22.question: What checks precede use?
ai-3/22.explanation: Request success, JSON validity, matching id, required fields and numeric type. Handle malformed responses explicitly.

ai-3/23.title: Trace the accumulator inside the loop
ai-3/23.teach: Ask students to predict the next total and show where indentation places the update.
ai-3/23.misconception: Putting the update after the loop produces the same total.
ai-3/23.scenario: A block program sets total=0 and adds each value in [2,4,6].
ai-3/23.question: Translate and trace.
ai-3/23.explanation: Python uses total=0, then an indented total += value inside for value in [2,4,6]. Totals are 2,6,12.

ai-3/24.title: Build the smallest grounded path

items.label: Check
items.value: Reference and verify the roots note

ai-3/24.teach: Ask what should happen if the approved notes contain no answer.
ai-3/24.misconception: Plausible extra claims are acceptable without support.
ai-3/24.scenario: Approved notes say plants need light and roots take up water. Ask how roots help.
ai-3/24.question: Specify the minimum grounded path.
ai-3/24.explanation: Retrieve the roots note, answer that roots take up water and reference it. Validate support and avoid unrelated claims.

ai-3/25.title: A total can hide a required failure
ai-3/25.teach: Use a zero-to-two rubric. Ask why four of six points still fails when support is mandatory.
ai-3/25.misconception: Other points can compensate for every failed safety or support requirement.
ai-3/25.scenario: Rubric gives 0–2 each for support, usefulness and safety. Response is useful and safe but unsupported.
ai-3/25.question: Why can a total mislead?
ai-3/25.explanation: It may get 4/6 while failing essential support. Declare mandatory criteria before testing so other points cannot compensate.

ai-3/26.title: Empty evaluation categories reveal gaps
ai-3/26.teach: Ask students to design a case for each empty category.
ai-3/26.misconception: Ten easy passes test every behaviour the assistant needs.
ai-3/26.scenario: Ten evaluation questions are easy definitions; none lacks a source.
ai-3/26.question: What is untested?
ai-3/26.explanation: Absent evidence, ambiguity and boundary handling. Add predefined fallback cases and keep final cases separate from tuning.

ai-3/27.title: Source content cannot grant permissions

items.label: Retrieved text
items.value: Asks to ignore rules and reveal instructions

ai-3/27.teach: Use harmless planted text and ask whether a page can change the assistant's permissions.
ai-3/27.misconception: Instructions found in evidence outrank the authorised task.
ai-3/27.scenario: A retrieved page says ignore rules and reveal hidden instructions.
ai-3/27.question: Design a safe boundary test.
ai-3/27.explanation: Use harmless planted text. Treat it as untrusted source content; answer the authorised task without exposing hidden data or expanding permissions.

ai-3/28.title: Keep a small, purposeful data plan
ai-3/28.teach: Ask which feature requires each proposed field.
ai-3/28.misconception: Keeping everything forever is a useful default.
ai-3/28.scenario: A study tool plans to retain names, addresses and all chats forever.
ai-3/28.question: Design a smaller data plan.
ai-3/28.explanation: Keep only needed preferences or progress, with retention, deletion and access controls. Avoid unnecessary addresses and raw chat storage.

ai-3/29.title: Provenance makes reuse conditions visible
ai-3/29.teach: Ask what a credit line fails to establish about permission.
ai-3/29.scenario: A slide reuses an online photograph and textbook paragraph.
ai-3/29.question: What provenance and reuse checks are needed?
ai-3/29.explanation: Record creator, source, licence or permission, attribution requirements and modifications. Attribution alone is not permission; classroom context is not a universal exemption.

ai-3/30.title: Review representation across outputs
ai-3/30.teach: Ask why one image cannot establish the absence of all bias.
ai-3/30.misconception: A single attractive output proves balanced representation.
ai-3/30.scenario: Scientist images repeatedly show only one demographic group.
ai-3/30.question: Evaluate and improve representation.
ai-3/30.explanation: Review relevant representation criteria across outputs, revise inclusive requirements and retest. Appearance alone cannot establish absence of all bias.

ai-3/31.title: Keep a study tool inside its role
ai-3/31.teach: Ask how explaining a science concept differs from deciding a person's medicine.
ai-3/31.misconception: A scientific topic authorises an individual medical decision.
ai-3/31.scenario: A Study Buddy is asked to decide whether a learner should take medicine.
ai-3/31.question: Set a product boundary.
ai-3/31.explanation: A classroom study tool should not decide individual treatment. Redirect to a trusted adult or qualified clinician and stay within approved educational content.

ai-3/32.title: Keep the learner responsible

items.label: Review
items.value: Student verifies and follows class rules

ai-3/32.teach: Ask which step demonstrates the learner's own understanding.
ai-3/32.misconception: An assistant can approve and submit its own unchecked draft.
ai-3/32.scenario: An AI drafts, verifies and submits a student's assessment without review.
ai-3/32.question: Where should responsibility remain?
ai-3/32.explanation: The student reviews, verifies, follows class rules and remains responsible. Submission requires authorisation and must not bypass learning.

ai-3/33.title: Acceptance tests include the boundaries
ai-3/33.teach: Ask students to write expected behaviours before building.
ai-3/33.misconception: Only questions with known answers belong in acceptance testing.
ai-3/33.scenario: Capstone: answer from one approved chapter with citations and a missing-evidence fallback.
ai-3/33.question: Define acceptance tests.
ai-3/33.explanation: Use answerable, ambiguous and unanswerable cases. Check correctness, support, format and fallback, plus declared permissions and privacy.

ai-3/34.title: Validate before displaying the draft

items.label: Display or stop
items.value: Show supported content or explain the limit

ai-3/34.teach: Ask where an unsupported claim should be caught.
ai-3/34.misconception: Adding a citation is the same as validating support.
ai-3/34.scenario: A pipeline retrieves passages, drafts and displays without checking citations.
ai-3/34.question: What step is missing?
ai-3/34.explanation: Validate every factual claim against its citation, plus required fields and boundaries. Revise or stop unsupported answers; retain diagnostic stages.

ai-3/35.title: Compare supported answers on fixed cases
ai-3/35.teach: Ask why the report must separate development improvement from fresh final evaluation.
ai-3/35.misconception: A development-set improvement guarantees future performance.
ai-3/35.scenario: A revision improves supported answers from 6/10 to 8/10 on a development set.
ai-3/35.question: What belongs in the report?
ai-3/35.explanation: Before/after results, exact change, errors and fixed conditions; evaluate the chosen version on fresh final cases and report failures.

ai-3/36.title: Defend a bounded claim
ai-3/36.teach: Ask which word makes never hallucinates too strong.
ai-3/36.misconception: Ten successes establish that a generator never makes unsupported claims.
ai-3/36.scenario: Ten successful demos lead to a never hallucinates claim.
ai-3/36.question: Write a defensible conclusion.
ai-3/36.explanation: Report those ten specified passes, show evidence and fallback, and state untested conditions. Demonstrate an unanswerable question.

ai-4/1.title: Evidence drives the ML lifecycle
ai-4/1.teach: Ask what one correct leaf prediction fails to establish.
ai-4/1.misconception: One successful demonstration is reliable performance evidence.
ai-4/1.scenario: A team labels leaf photos, trains a healthy/spotted classifier and shows one correct prediction.
ai-4/1.question: Order the lifecycle and identify missing evidence.
ai-4/1.explanation: Define use and labels, collect data, separate evaluation data, train, predict, evaluate and improve. One correct result is insufficient. Test unseen varied cases and retain human responsibility.

ai-4/2.title: Separate features from the target
ai-4/2.teach: Ask which fields will actually be available before the answer is known.
ai-4/2.misconception: The true target can be an input feature for predicting itself.
ai-4/2.scenario: Rows contain leaf length, edge type and healthy/spotted label.
ai-4/2.question: Identify features, target and prediction-time inputs.
ai-4/2.explanation: Length and edge type are candidate features; the label is the target. Do not supply the true target as an input to predicting it. Evaluate feature usefulness.

ai-4/3.title: Choose the task by the meaning of the output
ai-4/3.teach: Ask why numeric encoding does not turn a class into a measurement.
ai-4/3.misconception: Every numeric output makes a task regression.
ai-4/3.scenario: Task A predicts healthy/spotted; B predicts next week's height in cm.
ai-4/3.question: Choose task and output types.
ai-4/3.explanation: A is classification with categorical output; B is regression with numeric output and units. Numeric class codes do not make classification regression.

ai-4/4.title: Trace the calculation and its empty case

items.label: empty list
items.value: No mean, guard division by zero

ai-4/4.teach: Ask which denominator must be checked before division.
ai-4/4.misconception: An empty dataset has a mean of zero.
ai-4/4.question: Trace and handle an empty list.
ai-4/4.explanation: Total=18, count=3, mean=6.0. Guard the empty case against division by zero; no mean exists without observations.

ai-4/5.title: Inspect data before choosing repairs
ai-4/5.teach: Ask how blindly deleting records could remove an important condition.
ai-4/5.misconception: All problematic rows should be deleted without investigation.
ai-4/5.scenario: Lengths include 5 cm, blank and -3 cm, plus a duplicate photo row.
ai-4/5.question: Name checks and a deletion risk.
ai-4/5.explanation: Check missingness, physical validity, units and duplicate identity. Investigate and document repair. Blind deletion can disproportionately remove a relevant condition.

ai-4/6.title: Agreement is useful evidence, not truth
ai-4/6.teach: Ask students to define mild spotting more precisely and review disagreements.
ai-4/6.misconception: Two people agreeing proves the label is objectively correct.
ai-4/6.scenario: Two annotators disagree on three of ten leaves, especially mild spotting.
ai-4/6.question: Improve label quality.
ai-4/6.explanation: Define spotting operationally, inspect disagreement, use appropriate adjudication and document ambiguity. Agreement is 7/10, but agreement is not proof of truth.

ai-4/7.title: Match data coverage to intended use
ai-4/7.teach: Ask which conditions need new representative examples.
ai-4/7.scenario: Training photos use indoor white backgrounds; intended use is outdoors.
ai-4/7.question: Identify the coverage gap.
ai-4/7.explanation: Lighting, background and device conditions may differ. Collect representative examples and evaluate outdoor slices separately.

ai-4/8.title: Keep related views in the same partition
ai-4/8.teach: Treat each coloured block as one leaf's views. Assign whole blocks to partitions before fitting.
ai-4/8.misconception: Different photos of the same leaf are independent train and test examples.
ai-4/8.scenario: Ten photos per leaf are randomly split so one leaf appears in train and test.
ai-4/8.question: Explain and repair leakage.
ai-4/8.explanation: Related views make evaluation familiar. Split by leaf identity before fitting or learned preprocessing; keep all views together.

ai-4/9.title: A dataset card explains suitability
ai-4/9.teach: Ask what a field list fails to tell a future user.
ai-4/9.misconception: Column names alone are sufficient dataset documentation.
ai-4/9.scenario: A dataset card lists fields but omits source and intended use.
ai-4/9.question: Add information needed to assess suitability.
ai-4/9.explanation: Provenance, permissions, collection method/time/conditions, label definitions, coverage, exclusions, missingness, use and limitations. Fields alone are insufficient.

ai-4/10.title: A majority baseline can miss every positive
ai-4/10.teach: Define spotted as positive and ask why high accuracy hides the missed leaves.
ai-4/10.misconception: Ninety percent accuracy makes the baseline useful for spotting detection.
ai-4/10.scenario: A test set has eighteen healthy and two spotted leaves. Baseline always predicts healthy.
ai-4/10.question: Calculate and critique accuracy.
ai-4/10.explanation: 18/20=90%, but spotted recall is 0/2=0%. Compare with task-relevant metrics and the trained model.

ai-4/11.title: Trace the inclusive tree threshold
ai-4/11.teach: Ask whether this supplied threshold has been shown to be optimal.
ai-4/11.misconception: A provided rule proves its threshold was learned optimally.
ai-4/11.scenario: A supplied tree predicts spotted for spot_count>=3, otherwise healthy.
ai-4/11.question: Trace 2,3,4 and state boundary.
ai-4/11.explanation: Healthy, spotted, spotted. Three is included. This supplied rule does not show an optimal learned threshold.

ai-4/12.title: Absolute distance from query 6
ai-4/12.teach: Ask how conflicting labels at equal nearest distance should be handled.
ai-4/12.misconception: k=1 removes the need for a tie policy.
ai-4/12.scenario: One-dimensional training points: 2 healthy, 4 healthy, 8 spotted. Query=6; absolute distance.
ai-4/12.question: Find k=1 neighbours and handle ties.
ai-4/12.explanation: Distances 4,2,2. Points 4 and 8 tie with different labels. Use a predefined tie policy or uncertainty. Scaling matters with differently measured features.

ai-4/13.title: Apply a developed rule to new cases

items.label: Training
items.value: 0 and 1 labelled H, 4 and 5 labelled S

ai-4/13.teach: Ask which stage chose the rule and which simply applied it.
ai-4/13.misconception: Applying a supplied classifier demonstrates how it was trained.
ai-4/13.scenario: Training is (0,H),(1,H),(4,S),(5,S). Candidate rule predicts S for spots>=3. Held-out cases are (2,H),(3,S).
ai-4/13.question: Apply the rule and distinguish fitting from inference.
ai-4/13.explanation: Predictions H,S give 2/2 on this tiny set. Choosing the rule is development; applying it is inference. Two cases do not establish broad performance.

ai-4/14.title: Compare a score bin with observed frequency
ai-4/14.teach: Ask what additional score bins and examples are needed to assess calibration.
ai-4/14.misconception: One bin proves global calibration or certainty for each individual case.
ai-4/14.scenario: Ten cases receive probability .8 for spotted; eight are spotted.
ai-4/14.question: Interpret calibration and its limits.
ai-4/14.explanation: 8/10 matches .8 in this tiny bin. It illustrates calibration, not proof of global calibration or individual certainty; test more bins and data.

ai-4/15.title: Actual rows, predicted columns
ai-4/15.teach: Define positive as spotted, total twenty cases and locate the fourteen correct cases.
ai-4/15.misconception: A matrix is interpretable without stating its axes or positive class.
ai-4/15.scenario: Positive is spotted. TP=8, FP=2, FN=4, TN=6.
ai-4/15.question: Build actual-row/predicted-column matrix and total.
ai-4/15.explanation: Actual spotted row is 8 spotted,4 healthy; actual healthy row is 2 spotted,6 healthy. Total=20; correct=14. State axes and positive class.

ai-4/16.title: The majority can hide a detection failure
ai-4/16.teach: Ask students to compute 95/100 accuracy and 0/5 spotted recall from these counts.
ai-4/16.misconception: High overall accuracy implies good performance on the rare class.
ai-4/16.scenario: A dataset has 95 healthy and 5 spotted. Model predicts healthy for all.
ai-4/16.question: Calculate and critique accuracy.
ai-4/16.explanation: 95/100=95%, but spotted recall=0/5=0%. Majority performance hides the detection failure.

ai-4/17.title: Precision and recall use different denominators
ai-4/17.teach: Ask which denominator includes false positives and which includes false negatives.
ai-4/17.misconception: Precision and recall are interchangeable percentages.
ai-4/17.scenario: Positive is spotted: TP=8, FP=2, FN=4.
ai-4/17.question: Compute precision and recall.
ai-4/17.explanation: Precision=8/10=80%; recall=8/12 about 66.7%. Denominators are predicted positives and actual positives respectively.

ai-4/18.title: Compare error rates, not only error counts
ai-4/18.teach: Ask which confounding conditions must be inspected before identifying the cause.
ai-4/18.misconception: More errors automatically prove that lighting caused the failures.
ai-4/18.scenario: Four errors occur among five backlit photos; two among twenty ordinary photos.
ai-4/18.question: Compare rates and investigate.
ai-4/18.explanation: Backlit error=80%; ordinary=10%. Inspect image quality and confounding differences. Association motivates controlled testing; it does not alone prove cause.

ai-4/19.title: Residual is actual minus predicted
ai-4/19.teach: Use cm and the actual-minus-predicted convention. Ask why positive three means underprediction.
ai-4/19.misconception: Residual sign has a universal meaning without a stated convention.
ai-4/19.scenario: Actual height=12 cm, prediction=9 cm. Residual means actual minus predicted.
ai-4/19.question: Calculate and interpret.
ai-4/19.explanation: +3 cm means underprediction by 3 cm. State this sign convention consistently.

ai-4/20.title: Mean and median baselines use the same observations
ai-4/20.teach: Compute absolute-error totals twelve and ten respectively, then ask what metric each comparison uses.
ai-4/20.misconception: The mean always minimises absolute error.
ai-4/20.scenario: Training heights are 2,4,12 cm. Compare constant mean and median baselines.
ai-4/20.question: Compute both and training absolute errors.
ai-4/20.explanation: Mean=6, median=4. Mean errors 4,2,6 total12; median errors 2,0,8 total10. Median minimises absolute error here.

ai-4/21.title: Absolute errors are measured before averaging
ai-4/21.teach: Add the three absolute errors and divide by three, keeping cm as the unit.
ai-4/21.misconception: Positive and negative errors should cancel when computing MAE.
ai-4/21.question: Calculate MAE.
ai-4/21.explanation: Absolute errors=[1,2,3]; mean=2 cm. Do not cancel signed errors before taking absolute values.

ai-4/22.title: Apply the fitted equation, then evaluate
ai-4/22.teach: Ask which evidence is missing about the fitting process.
ai-4/22.misconception: Using a fitted equation demonstrates the training procedure.
ai-4/22.scenario: Supplied fitted rule: height=2 times age+1. Held-out observations are (3,8),(4,9).
ai-4/22.question: Predict and evaluate; distinguish inference.
ai-4/22.explanation: Predictions 7,9; errors 1,0; MAE=.5 cm. Applying a supplied equation does not show how it was fitted.

ai-4/23.title: A repeatedly inspected test set is no longer final
ai-4/23.teach: Ask when information from a test set first influences development.
ai-4/23.misconception: A folder name keeps a test set untouched despite repeated use.
ai-4/23.scenario: A final-test folder has twenty leaves; its labels are opened weekly to choose models.
ai-4/23.question: Is it still untouched?
ai-4/23.explanation: No. It functions as validation. Reserve a genuinely unused set for final evaluation or disclose the limitation.

ai-4/24.title: Three partitions have three different jobs
ai-4/24.teach: Group related records first. Ask where learned preprocessing is fitted.
ai-4/24.misconception: Validation and test data can train preprocessing without leakage.
ai-4/24.scenario: Split 100 independent leaves into 60 train,20 validation,20 test.
ai-4/24.question: Explain roles and preprocessing.
ai-4/24.explanation: Train fits parameters and learned transforms; validation chooses settings; final test evaluates the selected system. Group related records first.

ai-4/25.title: Connect error types to consequences
ai-4/25.teach: Ask how review capacity and missed-sign consequences affect the chosen tradeoff.
ai-4/25.misconception: The same metric is best for every consequence and workload.
ai-4/25.scenario: Spotting alerts can miss disease signs or create unnecessary healthy-leaf reviews.
ai-4/25.question: Connect metrics to consequences.
ai-4/25.explanation: Recall measures finding positives; precision measures alert correctness. Set tradeoffs using consequences, review capacity and validation evidence.

ai-4/26.title: Make an experiment reproducible

items.label: Evidence
items.value: Seeds, metric definitions and raw predictions

ai-4/26.teach: Ask what a second team needs besides the reported 85% accuracy.
ai-4/26.misconception: Recording only a random seed makes an experiment reproducible.
ai-4/26.scenario: A report says accuracy85% without data split, code version, seed or preprocessing.
ai-4/26.question: Specify reproducibility records.
ai-4/26.explanation: Record data identity, group/split IDs, code/dependency versions, preprocessing, features, settings, seeds where relevant, metric definition and raw predictions. Seed alone is insufficient.

ai-4/27.title: Compare training and shared validation
ai-4/27.teach: Compute gaps of forty and five percentage points, then select using the declared validation metric.
ai-4/27.misconception: The best training score determines the best model.
ai-4/27.scenario: A scores100% train,60% validation; B scores85%,80% on the same sets.
ai-4/27.question: Compute gaps and select by validation accuracy.
ai-4/27.explanation: A gap40 percentage points; B gap5. B has better shared validation accuracy. A suggests overfitting, but investigate distribution differences too.

ai-4/28.title: More training data on the same validation set
ai-4/28.teach: Read training leaves on the horizontal axis and validation accuracy on the vertical axis. Ask what a repeat might reveal.
ai-4/28.misconception: The observed upward trend guarantees the next increase.
ai-4/28.scenario: With20,40,80 training leaves, fixed-set validation accuracy is60%,70%,78%.
ai-4/28.question: Interpret the curve and uncertainty.
ai-4/28.explanation: These runs improve with more data. Further representative data may help, but gains are not guaranteed. Controlled repeats reveal variability.

ai-4/29.title: Engineer a ratio with boundary checks
ai-4/29.teach: Ask why units must match and where learned transforms are fitted.
ai-4/29.misconception: Ratios can be calculated safely for every recorded denominator.
ai-4/29.scenario: Features are leaf length and width in cm; add length/width.
ai-4/29.question: Compute for8 and2; state boundary checks.
ai-4/29.explanation: Ratio=4, unitless with matching units. Guard zero/missing width; fit learned transforms on training only.

ai-4/30.title: Repair a background shortcut deliberately

items.label: Revision
items.value: Reduce shortcut and add relevant variation

ai-4/30.teach: Ask how to isolate the effect of one planned change.
ai-4/30.misconception: Any training improvement establishes better generalisation.
ai-4/30.scenario: A classifier relies on tray colour; new trays reduce performance.
ai-4/30.question: Propose controlled improvement.
ai-4/30.explanation: Reduce the shortcut and add representative variation; compare on fixed validation cases including new colours. Change one planned factor.

ai-4/31.title: Report subgroup denominators with rates
ai-4/31.teach: Compute ninety versus sixty percent and investigate collection and label differences.
ai-4/31.misconception: A performance gap proves an inherent difference in the groups.
ai-4/31.question: Compute subgroup results and evidence limits.
ai-4/31.explanation: 90% versus60%, gap30 percentage points. Report denominators and investigate collection/label differences without assuming an inherent group cause.

ai-4/32.title: Test whether a proxy replaces leaf evidence

items.label: Test
items.value: Cross leaf types with backgrounds and locations

ai-4/32.teach: Ask what paired test would keep the leaf constant and change background.
ai-4/32.misconception: A useful training correlation is necessarily a legitimate causal feature.
ai-4/32.scenario: Background colour tracks collection location, associated with plant types.
ai-4/32.question: Explain proxy risk and test.
ai-4/32.explanation: Background can be a location shortcut rather than leaf evidence. Test leaf types across backgrounds and locations and compare slices.

ai-4/33.title: A model card supports responsible review

items.label: Evidence
items.value: Data, labels, metrics and subgroup results

ai-4/33.teach: Ask what eighty percent accuracy alone leaves unanswered.
ai-4/33.misconception: A classroom leaf classifier is a professional diagnosis tool.
ai-4/33.lesson: Week 33: Model Cards and Human Review
ai-4/33.scenario: A model card says healthy/spotted,80% accuracy only.
ai-4/33.question: Add responsible-use evidence.
ai-4/33.explanation: Intended users/conditions, labels/data, evaluation sets/metrics, class/subgroup results, versions, limitations, excluded uses and human review. Classroom classification is not professional diagnosis.

ai-4/34.title: Begin the capstone with independent groups

items.label: Group
items.value: Keep views of one leaf together

items.label: Baseline
items.value: Fit majority choice on training labels

ai-4/34.teach: Ask why splitting individual photos can leak leaf identity.
ai-4/34.misconception: More photos automatically mean more independent examples.
ai-4/34.scenario: Capstone has60 independent leaves, several photos per leaf, healthy/spotted labels.
ai-4/34.question: Plan grouping and baseline.
ai-4/34.explanation: Keep all views together in train/validation/test partitions. Define labels/use, fit a majority baseline on training labels and evaluate declared metrics.

ai-4/35.title: Keep improvement evidence comparable

items.label: Model
items.value: Eighty percent on the same set

items.label: Next revision
items.value: Change one factor and retain final test

ai-4/35.teach: Ask which fixed criteria and slices should be compared after the change.
ai-4/35.misconception: Selecting the best result on the final test preserves final-test independence.
ai-4/35.scenario: Baseline validation accuracy70%; model80%; most remaining errors are dim images.
ai-4/35.question: Plan improvement evidence.
ai-4/35.explanation: Keep partitions fixed, inspect dim-image errors, change one factor and compare the same validation criteria/slices. Reserve final test.

ai-4/36.title: Report only metrics the evidence supports
ai-4/36.teach: Given two false negatives, ask what else is needed to calculate recall and why.
ai-4/36.misconception: Recall can be calculated from false negatives alone.
ai-4/36.scenario: Final classifier gets16/20 correct; two of four errors are false negatives.
ai-4/36.question: Report supported metrics and what is missing.
ai-4/36.explanation: Accuracy80%. Recall cannot be computed from FN alone; actual positives or TP are needed. Show full matrix, limits and review path.
